title: Coins Have No Memory
objective: After this level you can explain what makes events independent and why a coin that landed heads five times is still 50/50.
summary: Independent events have no memory: after five heads, a fair coin is still 50/50. Six heads in a row is rare before you start (1 in 64), but so is every other sequence of six flips.

cards.headline: Heads, heads, heads, heads, heads. Is tails due?
cards.body: Almost everyone feels it is. Five heads in a row seems to call for a correction. Yet the coin about to be flipped is the same coin, with the same two faces, that you started with.

cards.headline: Independent means the past doesn't count
cards.body: Two events are independent if knowing that one happened doesn't change the chance of the other. Coin flips are the classic case: a coin is a disc of metal with nothing inside keeping score. So after five heads, the sixth flip is still 1 in 2 for heads. Dice work the same way: your first roll doesn't change the chances for your second.

cards.headline: Rare before, ordinary after
cards.body: Before you start, six heads in a row is rare: Level 23's multiplying gives 1 in 64. But once five heads have landed, that rarity is spent. The only thing left to decide is the sixth flip, and it's 50/50. In fact HHHHHH and HHHHHT are equally likely before you begin, and so is every other particular run of six flips: each is 1 in 64.

cards.context: Level 23's cards had real memory: keep hearts out of a deck and fewer hearts are left to draw. A coin has no deck to run down. So the law of averages does not say that after a run of heads, a head becomes less likely. Every flip starts from scratch.

mascot.line: Keep this: a streak is only rare before it happens. Once it's here, the next flip knows nothing about it.

cards.headline: Coins: no memory
learned: Six in a row: 1 in 64, like any run

questions.prompt: A fair coin has landed heads five times in a row. The chance the next flip is heads is _____.

options.label: less than 1 in 2
options.rationale: Tails is not "due"; the coin keeps no score.

options.label: more than 1 in 2
options.rationale: Heads is not "on a roll" either; each flip is fresh.

options.label: 1 in 64
options.rationale: 1 in 64 was the chance of six heads before any flips.

questions.explanation: Flips are independent, so the sixth flip is 1 in 2 whatever came before.

questions.prompt: How can six heads in a row be rare, yet a sixth head after five heads be 50/50?

options.label: The coin gets tired of landing heads
options.rationale: A coin has nothing inside it that tires or keeps score.

options.label: Once five heads have landed, only one 50/50 flip is left
Rare events become likely after a while
options.rationale: Chances of independent events never build up.

options.label: Six heads in a row is common, not rare
options.rationale: Before you start, six heads is 1 in 64: rare.

questions.explanation: Six heads is 1 in 64 before you start. After five heads, only the last flip remains, and it is 50/50.

questions.prompt: Why does keeping hearts out of a deck (Level 23) change the next draw, while a run of heads leaves the next flip alone?

options.label: Coins wear down on the side that lands most
options.rationale: Nothing about a fair coin changes from flip to flip.

options.label: Cards are about skill, coins about luck
options.rationale: Both are chance; the difference is what changes between tries.

options.label: Hearts are rarer than heads
options.rationale: How rare hearts are is not the point; the deck changing is.

options.label: The deck loses hearts; the coin loses nothing

questions.explanation: Drawing without replacement changes what is left in the deck. A coin has nothing to run down, so each flip starts fresh.
